claim: Plants typically release large quantities of volatiles in response to herbivory by insects.
source: Plants typically release large quantities of volatiles in response to herbivory by insects.
evidence: This is a well-established scientific fact supported by extensive literature in plant-insect interactions.

claim: Herbivore-induced plant volatiles benefit plants by attracting the natural enemies of the herbivores.
source: This benefits the plants by, for instance, attracting the natural enemies of the herbivores.
evidence: This is established knowledge in chemical ecology and is referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: BPH females preferentially oviposit on rice plants already infested by SSB.
source: BPH females preferentially oviposit on rice plants already infested by the rice striped stem borer (SSB), which are avoided by the egg parasitoid Anagrus nilaparvatae, the most important natural enemy of BPH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 showing oviposition preferences.

claim: SSB-infested rice plants are avoided by the egg parasitoid Anagrus nilaparvatae.
source: BPH females preferentially oviposit on rice plants already infested by the rice striped stem borer (SSB), which are avoided by the egg parasitoid Anagrus nilaparvatae, the most important natural enemy of BPH.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Anagrus nilaparvatae is the most important natural enemy of BPH.
source: BPH females preferentially oviposit on rice plants already infested by the rice striped stem borer (SSB), which are avoided by the egg parasitoid Anagrus nilaparvatae, the most important natural enemy of BPH.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lou et al., 2014 in the manuscript.

claim: The BPH oviposition strategy results in 80% lower parasitism rates of its eggs.
source: Moreover, greenhouse and field cage experiments confirm the adaptiveness of the BPH oviposition strategy, resulting in 80% lower parasitism rates of its eggs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from greenhouse and field cage experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: HIPVs serve as cues for natural enemies to locate their prey or hosts.
source: For instance, HIPVs serve as cues for natural enemies, such as predators and parasitoids, to locate their prey or hosts (Dicke et al., 2009; Allison and Daniel Hare, 2009; Allmann and Baldwin, 2010; Halitschke et al., 2008; Turlings and Erb, 2018; Schuman and Baldwin, 2018; Joo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: HIPVs play a role in repelling herbivores that avoid inducible plant defenses and conspecific or heterospecific competition.
source: They also play a role in repelling herbivores that avoid inducible plant defenses and conspecific or heterospecific competition (De Moraes et al., 2001; Knolhoff and Heckel, 2014; Anderson et al., 2011; Jiao et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HIPVs can attract specialist herbivores that aggregate to collectively overcome the defense of their hosts.
source: or they can attract specialist herbivores that aggregate to collectively overcome the defense of their hosts (Loughrin et al., 1995; Weed, 2010; Robert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HIPVs can be detected by neighboring plants and help them to anticipate an incoming attack.
source: HIPVs can also be detected by neighboring plants and help them to anticipate an incoming attack (Arimura et al., 2000; Heil and Ton, 2008; Engelberth et al., 2004; Karban et al., 2014; Sugimoto et al., 2014; Nagashima et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: BPH exhibits a strong preference for rice plants already infested by SSB.
source: We had found that BPH exhibits a strong preference for rice plants (Oryza sativa) that are already infested by the rice striped stem borer (SSB), Chilo suppressalis (Walker) (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018 and experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: BPH feeds on surface of rice plant stems.
source: BPH feeds on surface of rice plant stems, whereas SSB feeds inside the stems of rice plants (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: SSB feeds inside the stems of rice plants.
source: BPH feeds on surface of rice plant stems, whereas SSB feeds inside the stems of rice plants (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: There is only a minor direct effect on BPH development if they feed on SSB-infested rice plants relative to uninfested plants.
source: However, we only found a minor direct effect on BPH development if they feed on SSB-infested rice plants relative to uninfested plants (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Risk of predation or parasitism is an important factor influencing host selection behaviour of herbivores.
source: Risk of predation or parasitism is an important factor influencing host selection behaviour of herbivores (Denno et al., 1990; Holt and Lawton, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The natural enemies of BPH are known to be attracted to BPH-induced rice volatiles.
source: The natural enemies of BPH are known to be attracted to BPH-induced rice volatiles (Xiao et al., 2012; Lou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BPH females strongly preferred to settle on caterpillar-infested cultivated rice plants compared to uninfested plants.
source: When given a choice between uninfested rice and SSB-infested rice plants, the BPH females strongly preferred to settle on caterpillar-infested plants. This was the case for cultivated and for wild rice (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; all p<0.05) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BPH females strongly preferred to settle on caterpillar-infested wild rice plants compared to uninfested plants.
source: When given a choice between uninfested rice and SSB-infested rice plants, the BPH females strongly preferred to settle on caterpillar-infested plants. This was the case for cultivated and for wild rice (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; all p<0.05) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BPH adult females laid significantly more eggs on caterpillar-infested cultivated rice plants than on uninfested plants.
source: In concordance, BPH adult females laid significantly more eggs on caterpillar-infested rice plants than on uninfested plants (RT-test applied to a GLM, Piosson distribution error; all p<0.001) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BPH adult females laid significantly more eggs on caterpillar-infested wild rice plants than on uninfested plants.
source: In concordance, BPH adult females laid significantly more eggs on caterpillar-infested rice plants than on uninfested plants (RT-test applied to a GLM, Piosson distribution error; all p<0.001) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increasing BPH density positively correlated with the attraction of A. nilaparvatae wasps to infested plants.
source: Whether caterpillars were present or not, increasing the BPH density positively correlated with the attraction of the wasps to infested plants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the absence of SSB, A. nilaparvatae exhibited a preference for BPH-infested plants compared to insect free plants at densities of 5 and 10 BPH per plant.
source: In the absence of SSB, the parasitoid exhibited a preference for BPH-infested plants compared to insect free plants, although this was not significant at the lowest density of 2 BPH per plant (p=0.36, 0.002 and 0.001 at the density of 2, 5 and 10 per plant, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When 1 SSB caterpillar was present, A. nilaparvatae showed a strong preference for uninfested plants over plants infested with 0 or 2 BPH per plant.
source: When 1 SSB caterpillar was present, the parasitoids showed a strong preference for uninfested plants over infested plants either with 0 or 2 BPH per plant (p<0.001, in both cases), no significant preference with 5 BPH per plant (p=0.087), and significant preference for plants infested with 10 BPH over uninfested plants (p=0.001) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: With two SSB caterpillars present, A. nilaparvatae showed a strong preference for uninfested plants at densities of 0, 2 and 5 BPH per plant.
source: With two caterpillars present, the parasitoids showed a strong preference for uninfested plants at densities of 0, 2 and 5 BPH per plant (p<0.01 in all three cases), and no preference at the density of 10 BPH per plant (p=0.46) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A. nilaparvatae showed a strong preference for plants infested with 10 BPH over plants infested by 5 BPH.
source: As expected, the parasitoids showed a strong preference for plants infested with 10 BPH over plants infested by 5 BPH (p=0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The preference of A. nilaparvatae for plants with 10 BPH over 5 BPH was no longer observed when there was an SSB caterpillar present with the 10 BPH.
source: However, this preference was no longer observed when there was an SSB caterpillar present with the 10 BPH (p=0.87).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A. nilaparvatae exhibited a significant preference for plants infested by 5 BPH vs. plants infested by 10 BPH together with two caterpillars.
source: Moreover, the parasitoids exhibited a significant preference for plants infested by 5 BPH vs. plants infested by 10 BPH together with two caterpillars (p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A total of 41 compounds were detected in the headspace of uninfested rice plants.
source: A total of 41 compounds were detected in the headspace of uninfested rice plants, whereas 49 compounds were detected for rice plants damaged by BPH.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of volatile collections.

claim: 49 compounds were detected in the headspace of rice plants damaged by BPH.
source: A total of 41 compounds were detected in the headspace of uninfested rice plants, whereas 49 compounds were detected for rice plants damaged by BPH.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of volatile collections.

claim: 55 volatile compounds were detected when rice plants were infested by SSB only.
source: The number of detected volatile compounds increased to 55 when the rice plants were infested by SSB only, or by both SSB and BPH.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of volatile collections.

claim: 55 volatile compounds were detected when rice plants were infested by both SSB and BPH.
source: The number of detected volatile compounds increased to 55 when the rice plants were infested by SSB only, or by both SSB and BPH.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of volatile collections.

claim: The relative quantities of specific volatile compounds were significantly different among different plant treatments.
source: The relative quantities of specific compounds were significantly different among different plant treatments (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of GC-MS data.

claim: PLS-DA using the contents of all detected volatiles showed a clear separation between herbivore-infested treatments and uninfested control plants.
source: A projection to partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) using the contents of all detected volatiles showed a clear separation between herbivore-infested treatments and uninfested control plants, as well as between herbivore-treatments with or without SSB (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on PLS-DA analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The first two significant PLS components explained 30.8% and 10.3% of the total variance, respectively.
source: The first two significant PLS components explained 30.8% and 10.3% of the total variance, respectively.
evidence: This is based on PLS-DA analysis.

claim: The first PLS component showed a clear separation between volatile profiles of plants with SSB infestation versus the other two treatments.
source: The first component showed a clear separation between volatile profiles of plants with SSB infestation versus the other two treatments, while the second component separated volatile profiles released by plants infested by BPH only versus the other four treatments (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on PLS-DA analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The second PLS component separated volatile profiles released by plants infested by BPH only versus the other four treatments.
source: The first component showed a clear separation between volatile profiles of plants with SSB infestation versus the other two treatments, while the second component separated volatile profiles released by plants infested by BPH only versus the other four treatments (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on PLS-DA analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The first two PLS components could not separate the plants infested by SSB only or by SSB plus BPH.
source: However, the first two components could not separate the plants infested by SSB only or by SSB plus BPH.
evidence: This is based on PLS-DA analysis.

claim: The volatile blends emitted by the plants of the three SSB treatments contained the same number and type of volatile compounds.
source: The volatile blends emitted by the plants of the three SSB treatments contained the same number and type of volatile compounds, and only a few of them showed significant difference in relative amount (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis.

claim: 2-nonanone had a significant repellent effect on A. nilaparvatae wasps at either low or high dose or both doses.
source: Seven compounds, 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, (E)−2-heptany1 acetate, 2-heptanol, D-limonene, α-pinene and isopropyl myristate, had a significant repellent effect on the wasps compared to the control (hexane) at either low or high dose or both doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 2-tridecanone had a significant repellent effect on A. nilaparvatae wasps at either low or high dose or both doses.
source: Seven compounds, 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, (E)−2-heptany1 acetate, 2-heptanol, D-limonene, α-pinene and isopropyl myristate, had a significant repellent effect on the wasps compared to the control (hexane) at either low or high dose or both doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

source: Seven compounds, 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, (E)−2-heptany1 acetate, 2-heptanol, D-limonene, α-pinene and isopropyl myristate, had a significant repellent effect on the wasps compared to the control (hexane) at either low or high dose or both doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

source: Seven compounds, 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, (E)−2-heptany1 acetate, 2-heptanol, D-limonene, α-pinene and isopropyl myristate, had a significant repellent effect on the wasps compared to the control (hexane) at either low or high dose or both doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: α-pinene had a significant repellent effect on A. nilaparvatae wasps at either low or high dose or both doses.
source: Seven compounds, 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, (E)−2-heptany1 acetate, 2-heptanol, D-limonene, α-pinene and isopropyl myristate, had a significant repellent effect on the wasps compared to the control (hexane) at either low or high dose or both doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Isopropyl myristate had a significant repellent effect on A. nilaparvatae wasps at either low or high dose or both doses.
source: Seven compounds, 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, (E)−2-heptany1 acetate, 2-heptanol, D-limonene, α-pinene and isopropyl myristate, had a significant repellent effect on the wasps compared to the control (hexane) at either low or high dose or both doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: DMNT significantly attracted A. nilaparvatae wasps at both low and high doses.
source: In contrast, five compounds, DMNT, (E)-β-caryophyllene, linalool, methyl salicylate and (E)−2-hexenal, significantly attracted the wasps at both low and high doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: (E)-β-caryophyllene significantly attracted A. nilaparvatae wasps at both low and high doses.
source: In contrast, five compounds, DMNT, (E)-β-caryophyllene, linalool, methyl salicylate and (E)−2-hexenal, significantly attracted the wasps at both low and high doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Linalool significantly attracted A. nilaparvatae wasps at both low and high doses.
source: In contrast, five compounds, DMNT, (E)-β-caryophyllene, linalool, methyl salicylate and (E)−2-hexenal, significantly attracted the wasps at both low and high doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Methyl salicylate significantly attracted A. nilaparvatae wasps at both low and high doses.
source: In contrast, five compounds, DMNT, (E)-β-caryophyllene, linalool, methyl salicylate and (E)−2-hexenal, significantly attracted the wasps at both low and high doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: (E)−2-hexenal significantly attracted A. nilaparvatae wasps at both low and high doses.
source: In contrast, five compounds, DMNT, (E)-β-caryophyllene, linalool, methyl salicylate and (E)−2-hexenal, significantly attracted the wasps at both low and high doses.
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A. nilaparvatae females were attracted to TMTT at a low dose, but were repelled at a high dose.
source: Interestingly, A. nilaparvatae females were attracted to TMTT at a low dose, but were repelled at a high dose (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 73.1% of A. nilaparvatae females chose the synthetic blend that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 10 BPH females compared to the control.
source: There was a significantly higher percentage (73.1%) of A. nilaparvatae females that chose the synthetic blend that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 10 BPH females compared to the control (only hexane) (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Significantly fewer A. nilaparvatae parasitoids (30.4%) chose the synthetic blends that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 2 SSB caterpillars.
source: By contrast, significantly fewer parasitoids chose the synthetic blends that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 2 SSB caterpillars (30.4%; p<0.001) or two caterpillars plus 5 BPH females (37.3%; p=0.016).
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Significantly fewer A. nilaparvatae parasitoids (37.3%) chose the synthetic blends that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by two caterpillars plus 5 BPH females.
source: By contrast, significantly fewer parasitoids chose the synthetic blends that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 2 SSB caterpillars (30.4%; p<0.001) or two caterpillars plus 5 BPH females (37.3%; p=0.016).
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No significant effect on A. nilaparvatae parasitoid preference was detected for the synthetic blend that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 2 caterpillars plus 10 BPH females.
source: No significant effect on parasitoid preference was detected for the synthetic blend that mimicked the volatiles emitted by plants infested by 2 caterpillars plus 10 BPH females (p=0.33) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the greenhouse experiment, the mean numbers of BPH eggs laid on rice plants were not significantly different between plant treatments (10 BPH vs. 10 BPH + 1 SSB).
source: In this no-choice situation, the mean numbers of BPH eggs laid on rice plants were not significantly different between plant treatments (10 BPH vs. 10 BPH + 1 SSB, p=0.68; 10 BPH vs. 10 BPH + 2 SSB, p=0.69) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the greenhouse experiment, the mean numbers of BPH eggs laid on rice plants were not significantly different between plant treatments (10 BPH vs. 10 BPH + 2 SSB).
source: In this no-choice situation, the mean numbers of BPH eggs laid on rice plants were not significantly different between plant treatments (10 BPH vs. 10 BPH + 1 SSB, p=0.68; 10 BPH vs. 10 BPH + 2 SSB, p=0.69) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the greenhouse experiment, the rate of parasitism of BPH eggs was considerably lower on plants infested with 10 BPH plus 1 SSB than on plants infested with BPH only.
source: Still, the rate of parasitism of BPH eggs was considerably lower on plants infested with 10 BPH plus 1 SSB or 2 SSB than on plants infested with BPH only (both p<0.01) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the greenhouse experiment, the rate of parasitism of BPH eggs was considerably lower on plants infested with 10 BPH plus 2 SSB than on plants infested with BPH only.
source: Still, the rate of parasitism of BPH eggs was considerably lower on plants infested with 10 BPH plus 1 SSB or 2 SSB than on plants infested with BPH only (both p<0.01) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the field cage experiment, gravid BPH females exhibited a significant oviposition preference for rice plants infested with both herbivores as compared to plants infested with only BPH, with three times as many eggs on the doubly infested plants.
source: As expected from the earlier results (Figure 2), they exhibited a significant oviposition preference for rice plants infested with both herbivores as compared to plants infested with only BPH, with three times as many eggs on the doubly infested plants (p=0.004) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the field cage experiment, BPH eggs were parasitized far less (over 5-fold reduction) on plants infested with both herbivore species than on plants infested with BPH only.
source: Also, under these conditions, the BPH eggs were parasitized far less (over 5-fold reduction) on plants infested with both herbivore species than on plants infested with BPH only (p=0.005) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: SSB-induced volatiles dominate the plants' headspace and may thereby mask the BPH-induced volatiles.
source: PLS-DA of the volatiles revealed a clear separation between volatile profiles of plants with SSB infestation versus plants infested by BPH alone, but found no separation between plants infested by SSB only or by SSB plus BPH (Figure 4). This implies that SSB-induced volatiles dominate the plants' headspace and may thereby mask the BPH-induced volatiles.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLS-DA results showing no separation between SSB-only and SSB+BPH treatments.

claim: (E)−2-heptenyl acetate was only emitted by rice plants with SSB infestation.
source: Indeed, we identified (E)−2-heptenyl acetate as a compound that was only emitted by rice plants with SSB infestation, and it exhibited significant repellence to A. nilaparvatae (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis and Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: (E)−2-heptenyl acetate exhibited significant repellence to A. nilaparvatae.
source: Indeed, we identified (E)−2-heptenyl acetate as a compound that was only emitted by rice plants with SSB infestation, and it exhibited significant repellence to A. nilaparvatae (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by Y-tube assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The concentrations of 2-nonanone, 2-tridecanone, 2-heptanol, D-limonene and α-pinene were significantly increased upon SSB infestation.
source: These compounds were also emitted by uninfested plants or plants infested by BPH only, but their concentrations were significantly increased upon SSB infestation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For a highly specialized parasitoid like A. nilaparvatae, responses to volatile cues are expected to be innate and not easily changed through experience.
source: It is expected that for a highly specialized parasitoid like A. nilaparvatae these responses are innate and not easily changed through experience (Steidle and van Loon, 2003; Guo and Wang, 2019), unlike in generalist parasitoids, which are notoriously good learners and adapt their responses to odor cues depending on positive or negative host location experiences (Vet et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on parasitoid behavior.

claim: Generalist parasitoids are notoriously good learners and adapt their responses to odor cues depending on positive or negative host location experiences.
source: It is expected that for a highly specialized parasitoid like A. nilaparvatae these responses are innate and not easily changed through experience (Steidle and van Loon, 2003; Guo and Wang, 2019), unlike in generalist parasitoids, which are notoriously good learners and adapt their responses to odor cues depending on positive or negative host location experiences (Vet et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vet et al., 1995.

claim: SSB infestation did not suppress volatile compounds that are normally induced by BPH feeding.
source: Yet, in the current study we did not find any evidence that the emission of parasitoid-attractive compounds was suppressed by SSB infestation.
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of volatile emissions.

claim: SSB infestation increased most parasitoid-attractive compounds, just like the parasitoid-repellent compounds.
source: In fact, SSB infestation increased most of these attractants, just like the parasitoid-repellent compounds (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Changes in the overall composition and relative ratios of the volatile blend make plants that are co-infested by BPH and SSB unattractive to the parasitoid.
source: This implies that changes in the overall composition and relative ratios of the volatile blend make plants that are co-infested by BPH and SSB unattractive to the parasitoid.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of volatile analysis and behavioral assays.

claim: Adding whiteflies to spider mite infested lima bean plants results in a reduction in the emission of (E)-β-ocimene, thereby reducing the plants' attractiveness to predatory mites.
source: For example, adding whiteflies to spider mite infested lima bean plants results in a reduction in the emission of (E)-β-ocimene, thereby reducing the plants' attractiveness to predatory mites (Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Adding slugs to wild Brassica rapa that are infested by Pieris brassicae caterpillars results in an overall reduction in volatile emissions, leading to a reduced attraction of Cotesia glomerata.
source: Similarly, adding slugs to wild Brassica rapa that are infested by Pieris brassicae caterpillars results in an overall reduction in volatile emissions, leading to a reduced attraction of Cotesia glomerata (Desurmont et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Desurmont et al., 2016.

claim: When the exotic noctuid Spodoptera littoralis co-infests Brassica rapa plants that are under attack by native Pieris brassicae caterpillars, the dually-infested plants are considerably less attractive to the braconid wasp Cotesia glomerata.
source: For instance, when the exotic noctuid Spodoptera littoralis co-infests Brassica rapa plants that are under attack by native Pieris brassicae caterpillars, the dually-infested plants are considerably less attractive to the braconid wasp Cotesia glomerata, the main parasitoid of P. brassicae (Chabaane et al., 2015; Desurmont et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chabaane et al., 2015 and Desurmont et al., 2016.

claim: When spider mite-infested lima bean plants are also infested by whitefly nymphs this results in a reduced attraction of predatory mites.
source: Similarly, Zhang et al., 2009 reported that when spider mite-infested lima bean plants are also infested by whitefly nymphs this results in a reduced attraction of predatory mites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: Females of the moth P. xylostella preferentially oviposit on P. rapae-infested cabbage plants on which the parasitism rates of P. xylostella larvae by C. plutellae wasps are significantly reduced.
source: As in our study, Shiojiri et al., 2002 found that females of the moth P. xylostella preferentially oviposit on P. rapae -infested cabbage plants on which the parasitism rates of P. xylostella larvae by C. plutellae wasps are significantly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shiojiri et al., 2002.

claim: The lower parasitism rates on rice plants infested by both herbivores are caused by reduced attractiveness or even repellence by HIPVs released by SSB-infested rice plants.
source: These results were well in accordance with the preferences that the parasitoid showed in the olfactometer experiments, implying that the lower parasitism rates on rice plants infested by both herbivores are caused by reduced attractiveness or even repellence by HIPVs released by SSB-infested rice plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of olfactometer and parasitism experiments.
